Marvell and Intel have both lost more than half their value since June. At Tuesday's close on Nov 17, Marvell stood at $148.74. That is 53.0% below its high close of $316.43 on June 4. Intel closed at $55.17, 60.9% below its June 22 high. Most talk about the chip selloff is a buy-the-dip call or a warning that the AI trade is over. This article asks a narrower question. When a chip stock halves, how often does it get back to its high, and how long does it take?

Mostly they do come back, but the wait has ranged from months to decades. We looked at 20 chip stocks listed today, with daily prices since 1999. They had 57 falls of 50% or more from a high close. In 49 of them, the stock later closed back at or above the old high. The big difference is timing. Falls from highs set in 2002 or later took a median 1.2 years to recover. Falls from the dot-com highs took a median 16.4 years.

Intel is the clearest example. It halved from its August 2000 high and only closed back above it on April 24, 2026. That took 25.5 years. In June it set a new high of $140.94. Since Oct 30 it has been halved again.

This question sits inside the larger AI story we follow every day.

How We Counted A Halving

The test uses closing prices adjusted for stock splits. A fall starts on the first close at least 50% below the highest close so far. It ends when the stock closes at or above that high again. We measure the wait from that first close 50% down. One limit matters. The list holds only companies that are still listed. Chip companies that were bought out or delisted are not in it. We think that makes the true recovery rate for all chip stocks lower than these numbers. Adding dividends barely changes the result. On that basis, 49 of 57 falls still recovered.

Two Very Different Kinds Of Crash

Across all the falls, quick recoveries were rare. Of the halvings at least a year old, 24.0% got back to the high within a year. Of those at least five years old, 47.1% got back within five years. Those totals hide two very different groups.

The dot-com group fell much further. Every one of its 21 falls recovered in the end. But most of them took more than ten years. Micron needed 21.3 years. AMD needed 19.3 years.

Later falls were shallower and shorter. The chip peak of late 2021 is the closest recent test. Eight chip stocks halved from highs set between September 2021 and January 2022. All eight got back to the high, in 1.0 to 3.2 years. Nvidia took 1.0 years and Marvell took 2.4 years.

Nvidia doesn't just sell the chips behind the AI buildout. It also owns big stakes in the companies doing the building, and its 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30, filed Nov. 16, shows $48.33 billion of US stocks across eight positions.

Those stakes matter more than usual right now. Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on Nov. 12, and The Wall Street Journal reported that interim CEO Colette Kress is expected to pull back on the computing deals and startup investments Nvidia has been financing.

Of Nvidia's positions worth 2% or more, these are the five where Wall Street sees the most upside: CoreWeave (CRWV:NASDAQ), SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ), Coherent (COHR:NYSE), Intel (INTC:NASDAQ) and Synopsys (SNPS:NASDAQ). Together, they made up nearly 98% of the portfolio at Sept. 30.

title: What Sent Intel Stock Lower Since May?

What Sent Intel Stock Lower Since May?

Intel (INTC) stock fell 53.4% between May 21 and November 17, 2026, while the S&P 500 slipped 0.9% over the same dates. The shares first climbed to a $140.94 close on June 22. By the October 29 close, they had slid to $92.07, 22% below the May 21 close. The steepest day came next: a 28.6% drop on October 30, the session after Intel's October 29 earnings call. The stock then lost another 16% by the November 17 close. On the October 29 call, management said strong data center momentum was partly offset by weakness in PC chips. So what did the call show about each business?

Intel Expects Its PC Chip Sales To Fall Further

Management reported third-quarter PC chip revenue of $8.1 billion. That was down 9% from the second quarter and below the company's own expectations. Executives blamed higher memory prices and limited IT budgets. They expect PC chip revenue to fall more than 20% from the third quarter to the fourth.

This matters because PC chips were Intel's largest business, delivering $32.2 billion of revenue in fiscal 2025. Management now expects industry-wide PC unit sales to fall about 12% in 2026 and roughly 10% in 2027.

Management reported third-quarter revenue of $16.5 billion and guided the fourth quarter to $15 billion to $16 billion. That guide includes about $300 million of lost sales. An accident in early October led to an extended shutdown at Intel's Israel factory.

Management Does Not Expect Positive Cash Flow In 2027

Management called 2027 an investment year. Gross capital spending is set to rise strongly from the $20 billion Intel is on track to spend in 2026. Management said it does not expect positive cash flow in 2027. Cash flow is already thin. Over the twelve months to September 26, Intel turned $59.9 billion of revenue into $3.77 billion of free cash flow.

Intel also reported a $12.0 billion net loss over those twelve months. Most of that loss came in the June quarter. Intel lost $11.0 billion that quarter even though it earned $1.97 billion of operating income. So the loss came from items below operating income.

The slide also started from a very high valuation. At the end of June, Intel was priced at 12.5 times its sales, higher than at every other quarter end since late 2016. At the November 17 close, buyers still paid 4.8 times sales, more than the 3.2 times for the S&P 500.

Intel's Data Center Sales Are Still Growing

Intel's server chips are still growing fast. Management said data center revenue was $7.3 billion in the third quarter, up nearly 80% from a year earlier. It said demand still meaningfully exceeds what Intel can supply. It guided that business to grow by a mid-teens percentage from the third quarter to the fourth. Almost all of the Israel factory hit falls on 10-nanometer server products.

title: SpaceX Is Now Nvidia's Biggest Stock Holding, Ahead of Intel. Here's What That Says About SpaceX.
detail:
SpaceX Is Now Nvidia's Biggest Stock Holding, Ahead of Intel. Here's What That Says About SpaceX.
Daniel Sparks, The Motley Fool
Wed, November 18, 2026 at 1:17 PM MST 5 min read
NVDA
INTC
SPCX
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) filed its quarterly list of stock holdings on Monday, Nov. 16, and there's a new name on top. As of Sept. 30, SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) was the chipmaker's biggest disclosed stake, worth around $19.7 billion, or 40.7% of the reported portfolio. Intel (NASDAQ:INTC), which led the list three months before, slid to second with 40.1%.

Nvidia owned around 130.5 million SpaceX shares at the end of September, up from about 122.8 million at the end of June. Meanwhile, it shrank its Intel stake by a quarter, to around 161.1 million shares. Intel's still the bigger holding by share count. SpaceX leads in value.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

It's tempting to take this as Nvidia betting more on SpaceX. But I think the filing says less about that than it seems -- and more about how much SpaceX's own plans rely on Nvidia.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Did Nvidia buy more SpaceX stock?

The filing (a Form 13F, the quarterly holdings report big investment managers send regulators) lists positions on one date. It doesn't say why a position changed.

And Nvidia had a way to get more SpaceX shares without buying any. It invested in artificial intelligence (AI) coding firm Cursor in late 2025. SpaceX later bought Cursor in a deal that closed on Aug. 14, paying Cursor's shareholders in SpaceX stock.

Some or all of the 7.7 million or so extra shares may have come from the deal. Neither company has said.

The bigger shift was on the Intel side. Nvidia's SpaceX stake lost value in the third quarter, dipping from around $21 billion to $19.7 billion as SpaceX's share price dropped. But its Intel stake fell far more, from around $30 billion to $19.4 billion, after Nvidia cut its position by about 54 million shares and Intel's share price slid.

Without the extra SpaceX shares, Intel would still have barely kept the top spot. In other words, SpaceX rose to first mainly because Nvidia shrank its Intel stake.

A small piece of SpaceX

For SpaceX, the stake's small. Nvidia's 130.5 million shares made up about 1% of the 13.6 billion or so SpaceX had outstanding in mid-October. At roughly $141 a share as I write, they're worth about $18 billion, versus a market value of about $1.9 trillion.

They don't come with much say, either. At the June initial public offering (IPO), CEO Elon Musk had about 82% of the total voting power.

Micron Technology (MU) stock returned 189% over the past twelve months, against 10.3% for the S&P 500. That is even after a 21.3% drop in the past month. You would be buying profits at their peak. Micron's net margin over its latest four fiscal quarters is 63.8%. That is its highest at any quarter end in our data, which start in fiscal 2017. So what could a share bought at today's price still make you over the next three years?

Micron Stock Would Be Worth About A Fifth More

Under this scenario, a Micron share bought today would be worth about 21.2% more three years from now, or about 6.6% a year. The model assumes revenue grows 30% a year, the highest rate it allows. It calculates the net margin at 70% of today's level plus 30% of its average at earlier quarter ends. Investors are also assumed to pay three-quarters of today's P/E. That is the lowest P/E the model allows. It applies because the assumed growth is far slower than Micron's recent pace.

All of that gain comes from Micron's revenue, which more than doubles in the scenario. The lower margin and the lower P/E each pull the value back down. In fiscal 2025, the year before the latest results, the Cloud Memory Business Unit became Micron's largest business, with revenue up 256.6% to $13.5 billion.

Micron Has To Sell More Memory At High Prices

Micron's own outlook points in that direction for now. In its September 30 results release, the company said AI-driven demand positions it for a record fiscal 2027. Management's guide for fiscal Q1 2027 forecasts revenue of $60 billion to $63 billion. That stands above the $54.2 billion reported for fiscal Q4 2026, though it covers a single quarter rather than a yearly pace.

Management said that guide assumes only single-digit growth in the amount of memory shipped from the quarter before. Management expects the market to stay tight through 2028, with start-up costs partly offsetting higher prices and a better product mix. It also expects margins to widen through the rest of fiscal 2027 as prices keep rising, though more slowly.

title: Why Micron's Cheap P/E Has Often Meant A Peak

Why Micron's Cheap P/E Has Often Meant A Peak

Today's big story: Anthropic IPO: Priced For 2031, Or 2036?

Micron Technology (MU) closed at $712.42 on Tuesday, Nov 17. That is 9.6 times its fiscal 2026 earnings per share. The common view is that a memory chip maker at a single-digit price-to-earnings ratio, or P/E, looks cheap. This article asks a different question. What has a P/E under 10 meant for Micron in the past?

The short answer is that it has more often marked an earnings peak than a bargain. We checked every month-end since January 1999. Some months had a P/E under 10 while earnings per share for the last four quarters were higher than a year earlier, as they are now. The median price return over the next year from those months was a loss of 13.2%. The stock was higher a year later in only 17 of 48 such months. Other low-P/E months came after earnings had already fallen. From those, the median return was a gain of 18.7%. The stock rose in 15 of those 16 months.

Our Nov 17 piece, Should You Buy Micron Stock At Under Ten Times Earnings?, found Micron at 9.6 times earnings, against 22.0 times for the median S&P 500 company. The next question is whether that low P/E has been a good signal before. On Micron's own record, a low P/E on fast-rising earnings has usually been the market pricing a peak. Nothing in the price has changed that picture since. Micron slipped 0.9% on Tuesday, and its P/E is still under 10.

Why A Low P/E Can Be A Warning

A P/E divides the share price by the last year's earnings per share. For most companies a low number means the stock is cheap. Memory chips are different. Micron's profit swings with chip prices. It ran an operating loss in fiscal 2023. In fiscal 2026 its operating margin was 74.6%.

When profit is near a high, the price can look cheap against it. Investors may be pricing the lower earnings they expect once the cycle turns. Micron's fiscal 2026 earnings per share were $74.33. That is 9.8 times the $7.59 of fiscal 2025. That jump puts Micron firmly in the rising-earnings group.

Six Episodes, Four Losses

Back-to-back months share most of their one-year windows, so counting by episode is fairer. We treat each run of back-to-back month-ends under 10 times earnings as one episode. Micron has had six before now. Its P/E did not fall under 10 at any month-end until July 2010.

Five of the six episodes began while earnings were higher than a year earlier. In five of the six, earnings a year later were lower than at the start. The stock was lower a year after the first month in four of the six.

Today's big story: Anthropic IPO: Priced For 2031, Or 2036?

Nvidia reported its third quarter on Tuesday, Nov 17, after the market close. Sales came to $115.8 billion. Colette Kress, the interim CEO, commented on the results. This article looks at one number in the report. It is gross margin, the share of each sales dollar left after the direct cost of making the product.

Yes, Nvidia's gross margin lead over AMD has shrunk. In early 2024 Nvidia kept 31.6 points more of each sales dollar than AMD did. In the latest quarters the gap was 20.9 points. That is 10.7 points less. Against Broadcom the lead fell from 16.1 points to 5.8 points over the same stretch. These figures use GAAP, the standard accounting rules companies report under.

The rivals did most of the closing. Nvidia's own margin slipped 3.5 points over that time. AMD's margin rose 7.1 points. Broadcom's rose 6.9 points. So the rivals got better faster than Nvidia got worse. And over the latest year, the lead barely moved. It narrowed 0.8 points against AMD. It widened 0.5 points against Broadcom.

How Big Is Nvidia's Lead Today?

Nvidia's GAAP gross margin was 74.8% in the three months to Oct 25. AMD's was 53.9% in the three months to Sep 26. Broadcom's was 69.1% in the three months to Aug 2. The table shows the lead over each rival at four points in time. The Broadcom column uses Nvidia's quarter to Jul 26, which lines up with Broadcom's quarter to Aug 2.

The table also shows a longer history. The lead over Broadcom is about where it stood at the start of 2015. The lead over AMD is narrower than it was then. Early 2024 stands out as the widest point in the table.

Broadcom needs one more note. Its cost of sales includes the write-down of companies it bought, called amortization of acquired intangibles. That came to $1,499 million in its latest quarter. Leave it out, and Broadcom's gross margin was 74.2%. On that basis, Nvidia's lead in its quarter to Jul 26 was 0.8 points.

What The New Guide Says

The fresh number in this report is Nvidia's outlook. It expects a gross margin of 71.0% to 72.0% in the current quarter. The middle of that range is 3.3 points below the quarter just reported. AMD has guided its fourth-quarter margin to about 55% on an adjusted basis.

If both companies land at the middle of their guides, Nvidia's lead over AMD would be 16.5 points. That is a guide, not a result. It is also on a different basis from the 20.9 points above. AMD's adjusted margin leaves out some costs that GAAP includes. So the two numbers should not be read as a straight drop.

Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) has reportedly started another round of layoffs as CEO Lip-Bu Tan works to lower costs and simplify the chipmaker's operations.

Employees posted on social media that they had lost jobs in Intel's global information technology organization, Business Insider reported. Intel said it regularly reviews staffing to match business priorities and gave no figure for the latest cuts.

Intel had 81,100 employees at the end of September, down from 85,100 at the end of 2025. Tan, who became CEO last year, has been reducing layers of management and shifting resources away from lower-priority projects. The September headcount predates the latest reported layoffs.

The cuts come as Intel's sales are recovering. Third-quarter revenue rose 21% from a year earlier to $16.5 billion. Intel Foundry, its chip manufacturing business, narrowed its operating loss to about $1.9 billion from $2.3 billion a year earlier.

The unit generated $411 million in external revenue, with most of the year-over-year increase coming from a one-time contract.

Investors Takeaway

The first question is whether the latest cuts are large enough to affect operating expenses. For the manufacturing turnaround, a more telling measure will be whether Intel can win repeat orders from outside chipmakers.

Recurring foundry revenue and a sustained decline in operating losses would give investors a clearer read on whether the factory business is gaining traction.
